No scientific evidence is available against any mechanism. We therefore introduce three genuinely new operator constructions that have not appeared in any prior attempt: (1) a graph-Laplacian-structured linear operator with a learnable sparse adjacency (a fundamentally different inductive bias — graph topology — from the dense or POD-banded structures previously tried), (2) a matrix-exponential parameterization of a continuous-time generator (a non-Euclidean parameterization, never explored here, that guarantees invertibility and exposes a natural multi-step rollout), and (3) a mass-conserving diffusion-reaction operator with an explicit 26-26 reactant/product block split (combines a hard conservation constraint with an explicit reaction term, a combination not present in any prior hypothesis, including the symplectic C002_H01 which used a much stronger single-form conservation). hypotheses.name: Graph-Laplacian-structured linear operator with learnable sparse adjacency
hypotheses.scientific_question: Are the 52D POD-latent dynamics well described by a (negative) graph-Laplacian diffusion on a learnable sparse interaction graph, rather than a dense linear map?
hypotheses.mechanism: The discrete-time linear operator is parameterized as A = -alpha * L - beta * I, where L = D - W is the graph Laplacian of a learnable symmetric, sparse adjacency W in R^{52x52}, alpha > 0 is a learnable scalar, and beta >= 0 is a learnable scalar shift. Sparsity is enforced either by a hard k-nearest-neighbor mask on W or by an L1 penalty with a target sparsity level. The dynamics are z_{t+1} = A z_t.
hypotheses.mathematical_form: Let W in R^{52x52} be symmetric, with W_ij = W_ji, and let D = diag(W 1) be the degree matrix. Define L = D - W. Then A = -alpha L - beta I, and z_{t+1} = A z_t. Equivalently, z_{t+1,i} = -alpha * sum_j W_ij (z_{t,i} - z_{t,j}) - beta z_{t,i}. Note: when W is non-negative this is a conservative diffusion on a weighted graph.
hypotheses.motivation: If the 52 latent modes interact primarily through a small set of pairwise couplings, the linear operator should be well approximated by a (negative) graph Laplacian rather than a dense matrix. The inductive bias is fundamentally different from: (a) a dense unconstrained linear operator, (b) a POD-energy-banded sparse operator (C003_H02), which band-sparsifies by energy ordering rather than by graph topology, and (c) symbolic sparsity (C002_H03), which uses generic sparsity. Graph-Laplacian structure enforces a real, non-positive spectrum, a localized interaction pattern, and a known interpretation in terms of diffusion on a network.
hypotheses.explanation_of_previous_failure: No prior hypothesis explored graph-Laplacian structure. The closest 'sparse linear' attempts (C003_H02 POD-energy-band, C002_H03 sparse symbolic) impose sparsity in a basis-index or symbolic-monomial sense, not via a learnable graph topology. C001_H02 'divergence-free' imposes a continuous-space vector-field constraint, not a discrete graph structure. The graph Laplacian is a genuinely new operator construction in this research line.
hypotheses.distinguishing_prediction: (i) The learned W is sparse: at least 70% of off-diagonal entries are below 1e-3 in magnitude. (ii) The eigenvalue spectrum of A is real (graph Laplacian has real spectrum), in contrast to a generic dense linear operator which generically has complex eigenvalues. (iii) The right eigenvectors of A are approximately constant on connected components of the graph defined by W, exhibiting community structure visible from a 2D embedding of the 52 modes. (iv) The one-step MSE on development_validation is at least as low as a dense linear baseline, and the multi-step rollout error grows more slowly due to the more constrained spectrum.
minimum_experiment: Train (W, alpha, beta) jointly on development_train by minimizing one-step squared error ||A z_t - z_{t+1}||^2, with an L1 penalty on off-diagonal entries of W targeting >= 70% sparsity.
Evaluate one-step MSE on development_validation; compare to a dense linear baseline (unconstrained A) trained on the same data.
Compute the spectrum of the learned A; report the fraction of real eigenvalues.
Visualize the support pattern of W as a 52x52 heatmap and report the number of connected components in the graph induced by thresholding W.
hypotheses.expected_observation_if_true: One-step MSE within 5% of the dense linear baseline; eigenvalue spectrum of A is at least 90% real; W has 1-4 connected components; multi-step rollout error grows slower than the baseline by at least 20% at rollout length 10.
hypotheses.expected_observation_if_false: One-step MSE is worse than baseline by more than 10%; the spectrum is predominantly complex (similar to a generic dense A); W is dense or has no clear community structure; multi-step rollout does not improve.
risks: Hard sparsity may be too restrictive; an L1-only penalty may produce a dense W that mimics a generic linear operator.
The graph Laplacian is symmetric, so A is symmetric up to the -beta I shift; if the true latent dynamics are strongly non-symmetric, this inductive bias is misspecified.
The 52 modes may not have a meaningful graph structure; the latent representation from POD is a flat vector without topology.
hypotheses.relation_to_existing_methods: Related to graph signal processing, graph neural networks, and graph-Laplacian-based dimensionality reduction (e.g., Laplacian eigenmaps). Not previously instantiated in this ROM pipeline. Distinct from C003_H02 (energy-band sparsity) and C002_H03 (symbolic sparsity) by the type of sparsity (graph-topological vs. basis-index vs. symbolic) and from C002_H01 (symplectic) by the conservation structure (graph-Laplacian conserves a sum, not a symplectic 2-form).

hypotheses.name: Continuous-time normal-form linear operator via matrix-exponential parameterization
hypotheses.scientific_question: Does parameterizing the discrete-time operator as the matrix exponential of a learnable continuous-time generator B (i.e., A = expm(B)) change the inductive bias and stability properties enough to outperform a directly parameterized A, given the same one-step training objective?
hypotheses.mechanism: Instead of learning A directly in R^{52x52}, we learn a continuous-time generator B in R^{52x52} and define A = expm(B). The discrete-time map is then z_{t+1} = expm(B) z_t. Training is performed with the same one-step squared error ||expm(B) z_t - z_{t+1}||^2 on development_train. The matrix exponential is computed at each training step (e.g., via a Pade approximation or scipy.linalg.expm in the forward pass). The multi-step rollout uses expm(k * B) for step k.
hypotheses.mathematical_form: B in R^{52x52} is the only learnable parameter. A = expm(B), so z_{t+1} = A z_t = expm(B) z_t. For multi-step rollouts, z_{t+k} = expm(k B) z_t. Stability: if max Re(lambda(B)) <= 0 then ||A||_2 <= 1, equivalently max Re(lambda(A)) <= 1, with strict inequality if B is Hurwitz.
hypotheses.motivation: Many physical systems, including fluid flows, are naturally described in continuous time. The matrix-exponential map is a different parameterization geometry from the Euclidean parameterization of a generic linear A: it (a) guarantees A is always invertible, with det(A) = exp(trace(B)) > 0, (b) provides a natural and numerically stable multi-step rollout via expm(k B) rather than repeated multiplication, and (c) exposes a more interpretable stability condition (Hurwitz property of B). This is a non-Euclidean parameterization, fundamentally different from the Euclidean parameterizations used in every prior linear-operator attempt (BOOTSTRAP_H1, C002_H02, C003_H01, C003_H02, C003_H03, H1, H2 from cycle 9 — note: H2 from cycle 9 was an RBF interpolation, not Cayley or exponential). The Cayley transform (A = (I-K)(I+K)^{-1}) is a related but distinct non-Euclidean parameterization that was also not explored; the matrix exponential is the natural map for continuous-time systems and is preferred here because it preserves the determinant and supports straightforward multi-step rollouts.
hypotheses.explanation_of_previous_failure: Every prior linear-operator attempt parameterized A directly in R^{52x52}. None used a non-Euclidean parameterization such as the matrix exponential or Cayley transform. C002_H01 (symplectic) imposed a constraint on A (J-orthogonality) but did not change the parameterization geometry. C003_H01 (Bayesian hierarchical-shrinkage) added a probabilistic prior but kept the Euclidean parameterization. The matrix-exponential parameterization is a genuinely new mechanism in this research line.
hypotheses.distinguishing_prediction: (i) The learned A always has det(A) > 0, in contrast to a generic dense A whose determinant can be of either sign. (ii) The continuous-time generator B has a small spectral radius (||B||_2 < 5 in the learned model), reflecting that the discrete-time step is 'close to identity' when the continuous-time dynamics are slow. (iii) The multi-step rollout error z_{t+k} = expm(k B) z_t grows more slowly than the repeated-multiplication rollout z_{t+k} = A^k z_t with the same A, because expm(k B) avoids the accumulation of numerical error from repeated matrix powers. (iv) The eigenvalues of A lie in the right half of the complex plane (since A = exp(B) and exp maps to C\{0}).
minimum_experiment: Train B on development_train to minimize one-step squared error ||expm(B) z_t - z_{t+1}||^2 using automatic differentiation through expm.
Evaluate one-step MSE on development_validation; compare to a dense linear baseline (unconstrained A) trained on the same data.
Compute det(A), the spectral radius of B, and the eigenvalues of A.
Compute the multi-step rollout error at horizons k = 1, 5, 10, 20 using both expm(k B) and A^k; report the ratio.
hypotheses.expected_observation_if_true: One-step MSE within 5% of the dense linear baseline; det(A) > 0; expm(k B) rollout has lower error than A^k rollout by at least 10% at k = 20; spectral radius of B is < 5.
hypotheses.expected_observation_if_false: One-step MSE is worse than baseline by more than 10%; det(A) is not consistently positive (suggesting that the parameterization is not the bottleneck); expm(k B) and A^k give similar rollout errors.
risks: Matrix-exponential computation is more expensive per step (Pade approximation or eigendecomposition) and may be a numerical bottleneck.
The training landscape of B (with a non-Euclidean loss) may have different optimization properties (more local minima, slower convergence) than direct parameterization of A.
If the true dynamics are genuinely discrete-time (not the discretization of a continuous-time flow), the matrix-exponential parameterization adds an unnecessary indirection.
hypotheses.relation_to_existing_methods: Related to Lie-group methods in deep learning (matrix exponential in RNNs, optimization on matrix manifolds), to geometric integration of ODEs, and to continuous-depth neural models. Distinct from C002_H01 (symplectic) and C003_H01 (Bayesian shrinkage) because the change is in the parameterization geometry, not in the constraint or prior.

hypotheses.name: Mass-conserving diffusion-reaction latent operator with explicit 26-26 reactant/product block split
hypotheses.scientific_question: Can the 52D latent dynamics be decomposed into a 26D 'reactant' block and a 26D 'product' block with a mass-conserving linear diffusion coupling between them and a learned (possibly nonlinear) reaction term, and does this decomposition outperform a generic linear operator on one-step and multi-step prediction?
hypotheses.mechanism: Split z = (z^R, z^P) in R^{26} x R^{26} via a fixed preprocessing assignment (e.g., based on the sign of the projection onto the first PCA direction, or based on a k-means partition in PCA space). The dynamics are: z^R_{t+1} = z^R_t - C(z^R_t, z^P_t) + R(z^R_t); z^P_{t+1} = z^P_t + C(z^R_t, z^P_t) - R(z^R_t). The 'mass' M_t = sum_i z^R_{t,i} + sum_i z^P_{t,i} is conserved by construction. C is parameterized as a linear diffusion D in R^{26x26} (constrained symmetric non-negative-definite via a Cholesky factor L_D, with D = L_D L_D^T), and R is a small learned function (e.g., a 2-layer MLP with 32 hidden units, or a quadratic form R(z) = diag(M_2 z) z with a learnable M_2 in R^{26x26}). The map is residual_operator compatible: z_{t+1} = A z_t + R_block(z_t) where A is a 52x52 matrix that implements the linear diffusion-reaction split and R_block is the nonlinear correction.
hypotheses.mathematical_form: Let P in R^{26x52} be a fixed 0/1 selection matrix that extracts the 'reactant' block, and Q = I - P^T P the complementary projector. Define the linear part: A = I - K + K^T, where K is a 52x52 block matrix K = [[0, 0], [D, 0]] for the linear diffusion D = L_D L_D^T. The full map is: z_{t+1} = A z_t + g(z_t), where g is a learnable function that satisfies sum(g(z)) = 0 for all z (so the mass M_t is preserved). The simplest choice is g(z) = (P^T - Q^T) R(P z), i.e., the reaction R acts on the reactant block and is subtracted from the reactant block and added to the product block. R: R^{26} -> R^{26} is a 2-layer MLP or quadratic form.
hypotheses.motivation: Reduced-order models of scalar-transport processes in fluids (e.g., mixing of a passive scalar, reaction-diffusion systems) have a natural decomposition into 'reactant' and 'product' blocks with a mass-conserving diffusion-reaction structure. If the 52D POD latent preserves some of this structure, a diffusion-reaction model with explicit block split and hard mass conservation should outperform a generic linear operator. The mass conservation is a hard structural constraint, not a soft penalty, and is a much weaker constraint than the symplectic 2-form preservation in C002_H01 (one constraint per 'mass' rather than O(n^2) constraints). The combination of block structure + hard conservation + learned reaction has not appeared in any prior hypothesis.
hypotheses.explanation_of_previous_failure: No prior hypothesis combined block structure with hard mass conservation and an explicit learned reaction term. C002_H01 (symplectic) imposed a stronger conservation (symplectic 2-form) without block structure or reaction. C001_H02 (divergence-free) is a continuous-space vector-field condition, not a discrete block-decomposition. C001_H03 (multi-scale) decomposed by time scale, not by mass block. C003_H03 (energy-decomposed linear + low-energy residual) decomposed by energy band, not by mass block. The diffusion-reaction construction is genuinely new here.
hypotheses.distinguishing_prediction: (i) The learned D is approximately symmetric and positive semi-definite (Cholesky factor is well-conditioned). (ii) The mass M_t = sum(z_t) is approximately conserved over a multi-step rollout of length 20, with relative drift < 1% per step, in contrast to a generic linear operator where the mass drifts by O(1) over the same horizon. (iii) The reaction term R has a non-trivial magnitude: ||R(z)|| / ||D z|| is at least 0.1 on training data, indicating the reaction is not negligible. (iv) The one-step MSE is at least as low as a dense linear baseline, and the multi-step rollout is significantly better because of the mass conservation.
minimum_experiment: Determine the 26-26 split on development_train via k-means (k=2) on the first 3 PCA components of the training latent states; fix the split.
Train (L_D, parameters of R) on development_train to minimize one-step squared error under the constraint sum(g(z)) = 0.
Evaluate one-step MSE on development_validation; compare to a dense linear baseline.
Compute the mass M_t on a 20-step rollout initialized from development_validation initial conditions; report the relative mass drift per step.
Compare the magnitudes of the diffusion term and the reaction term on training data.
hypotheses.expected_observation_if_true: One-step MSE within 5% of the dense linear baseline; mass drift < 1% per step over a 20-step rollout (versus > 5% for the baseline); reaction-to-diffusion magnitude ratio is in [0.1, 1.0]; D has condition number < 100.
hypotheses.expected_observation_if_false: One-step MSE is worse than baseline by more than 10%; mass drift is comparable to the baseline (suggesting the mass conservation is not the bottleneck); reaction term is negligible (||R||/||D|| < 0.01) or overwhelms diffusion (ratio > 10).
risks: The 26-26 split is a preprocessing choice; the wrong split may severely hurt performance and may not be discoverable from data without supervision.
Mass conservation is a hard constraint; if the true 52D dynamics do not conserve a linear mass, this hypothesis is misspecified and will underperform.
The reaction function R is an additional nonlinear component that may overfit if too expressive (e.g., a large MLP) or be insufficient if too simple (e.g., a single quadratic).
The diffusion D is symmetric, which is a strong constraint; real mass-conserving transport may have non-symmetric structure.
hypotheses.relation_to_existing_methods: Related to reaction-diffusion reduced-order models, mass-conserving neural networks (e.g., graph neural networks with conservative message passing), and block-structured linear operators in fluid ROM. Distinct from C002_H01 (symplectic, stronger conservation, no block split) and from C003_H03 (energy-band split, no conservation) by the combination of block structure with hard mass conservation and an explicit reaction term.

hypothesis.name: Mass-conserving diffusion-reaction latent operator with explicit 26-26 reactant/product block split
hypothesis.scientific_question: Can the 52D latent dynamics be decomposed into a 26D 'reactant' block and a 26D 'product' block with a mass-conserving linear diffusion coupling between them and a learned (possibly nonlinear) reaction term, and does this decomposition outperform a generic linear operator on one-step and multi-step prediction?
hypothesis.mechanism: Split z = (z^R, z^P) in R^{26} x R^{26} via a fixed preprocessing assignment (e.g., based on the sign of the projection onto the first PCA direction, or based on a k-means partition in PCA space). The dynamics are: z^R_{t+1} = z^R_t - C(z^R_t, z^P_t) + R(z^R_t); z^P_{t+1} = z^P_t + C(z^R_t, z^P_t) - R(z^R_t). The 'mass' M_t = sum_i z^R_{t,i} + sum_i z^P_{t,i} is conserved by construction. C is parameterized as a linear diffusion D in R^{26x26} (constrained symmetric non-negative-definite via a Cholesky factor L_D, with D = L_D L_D^T), and R is a small learned function (e.g., a 2-layer MLP with 32 hidden units, or a quadratic form R(z) = diag(M_2 z) z with a learnable M_2 in R^{26x26}). The map is residual_operator compatible: z_{t+1} = A z_t + R_block(z_t) where A is a 52x52 matrix that implements the linear diffusion-reaction split and R_block is the nonlinear correction.
hypothesis.mathematical_form: Let P in R^{26x52} be a fixed 0/1 selection matrix that extracts the 'reactant' block, and Q = I - P^T P the complementary projector. Define the linear part: A = I - K + K^T, where K is a 52x52 block matrix K = [[0, 0], [D, 0]] for the linear diffusion D = L_D L_D^T. The full map is: z_{t+1} = A z_t + g(z_t), where g is a learnable function that satisfies sum(g(z)) = 0 for all z (so the mass M_t is preserved). The simplest choice is g(z) = (P^T - Q^T) R(P z), i.e., the reaction R acts on the reactant block and is subtracted from the reactant block and added to the product block. R: R^{26} -> R^{26} is a 2-layer MLP or quadratic form.
hypothesis.motivation: Reduced-order models of scalar-transport processes in fluids (e.g., mixing of a passive scalar, reaction-diffusion systems) have a natural decomposition into 'reactant' and 'product' blocks with a mass-conserving diffusion-reaction structure. If the 52D POD latent preserves some of this structure, a diffusion-reaction model with explicit block split and hard mass conservation should outperform a generic linear operator. The mass conservation is a hard structural constraint, not a soft penalty, and is a much weaker constraint than the symplectic 2-form preservation in C002_H01 (one constraint per 'mass' rather than O(n^2) constraints). The combination of block structure + hard conservation + learned reaction has not appeared in any prior hypothesis.
hypothesis.explanation_of_previous_failure: No prior hypothesis combined block structure with hard mass conservation and an explicit learned reaction term. C002_H01 (symplectic) imposed a stronger conservation (symplectic 2-form) without block structure or reaction. C001_H02 (divergence-free) is a continuous-space vector-field condition, not a discrete block-decomposition. C001_H03 (multi-scale) decomposed by time scale, not by mass block. C003_H03 (energy-decomposed linear + low-energy residual) decomposed by energy band, not by mass block. The diffusion-reaction construction is genuinely new here.
hypothesis.distinguishing_prediction: (i) The learned D is approximately symmetric and positive semi-definite (Cholesky factor is well-conditioned). (ii) The mass M_t = sum(z_t) is approximately conserved over a multi-step rollout of length 20, with relative drift < 1% per step, in contrast to a generic linear operator where the mass drifts by O(1) over the same horizon. (iii) The reaction term R has a non-trivial magnitude: ||R(z)|| / ||D z|| is at least 0.1 on training data, indicating the reaction is not negligible. (iv) The one-step MSE is at least as low as a dense linear baseline, and the multi-step rollout is significantly better because of the mass conservation.
minimum_experiment: Determine the 26-26 split on development_train via k-means (k=2) on the first 3 PCA components of the training latent states; fix the split.
Train (L_D, parameters of R) on development_train to minimize one-step squared error under the constraint sum(g(z)) = 0.
Evaluate one-step MSE on development_validation; compare to a dense linear baseline.
Compute the mass M_t on a 20-step rollout initialized from development_validation initial conditions; report the relative mass drift per step.
Compare the magnitudes of the diffusion term and the reaction term on training data.
hypothesis.expected_observation_if_true: One-step MSE within 5% of the dense linear baseline; mass drift < 1% per step over a 20-step rollout (versus > 5% for the baseline); reaction-to-diffusion magnitude ratio is in [0.1, 1.0]; D has condition number < 100.
hypothesis.expected_observation_if_false: One-step MSE is worse than baseline by more than 10%; mass drift is comparable to the baseline (suggesting the mass conservation is not the bottleneck); reaction term is negligible (||R||/||D|| < 0.01) or overwhelms diffusion (ratio > 10).
risks: The 26-26 split is a preprocessing choice; the wrong split may severely hurt performance and may not be discoverable from data without supervision.
Mass conservation is a hard constraint; if the true 52D dynamics do not conserve a linear mass, this hypothesis is misspecified and will underperform.
The reaction function R is an additional nonlinear component that may overfit if too expressive (e.g., a large MLP) or be insufficient if too simple (e.g., a single quadratic).
The diffusion D is symmetric, which is a strong constraint; real mass-conserving transport may have non-symmetric structure.
hypothesis.relation_to_existing_methods: Related to reaction-diffusion reduced-order models, mass-conserving neural networks (e.g., graph neural networks with conservative message passing), and block-structured linear operators in fluid ROM. Distinct from C002_H01 (symplectic, stronger conservation, no block split) and from C003_H03 (energy-band split, no conservation) by the combination of block structure with hard mass conservation and an explicit reaction term.
